claim: Liver kinase B1 (LKB1), also known as serine/threonine kinase 11 (STK11), is the major energy sensor for cells to respond to metabolic stress.
source: Liver kinase B1 (LKB1), also known as serine/threonine kinase 11 (STK11) is the major energy sensor for cells to respond to metabolic stress.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about LKB1/STK11 function.

claim: Autophagy degrades and recycles proteins, macromolecules, and organelles for cells to survive starvation.
source: Autophagy degrades and recycles proteins, macromolecules, and organelles for cells to survive starvation.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that draws on established scientific knowledge about autophagy function.

claim: Lkb1 is essential for the survival of adult mice.
source: We found that Lkb1 was essential for the survival of adult mice, and autophagy activation could temporarily compensate for the acute loss of Lkb1 and extend mouse life span.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2a and described in the Results section.

claim: Autophagy activation can temporarily compensate for the acute loss of Lkb1 and extend mouse life span.
source: We found that Lkb1 was essential for the survival of adult mice, and autophagy activation could temporarily compensate for the acute loss of Lkb1 and extend mouse life span.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data comparing Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice leads to impaired intestinal barrier function.
source: We further found that acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice led to impaired intestinal barrier function, hypoglycemia, and abnormal serum metabolism, which was partly rescued by the Lkb1 loss-induced autophagy upregulation via inhibiting p53 induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by FITC-dextran permeability assay data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: Acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice leads to hypoglycemia.
source: We further found that acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice led to impaired intestinal barrier function, hypoglycemia, and abnormal serum metabolism, which was partly rescued by the Lkb1 loss-induced autophagy upregulation via inhibiting p53 induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 5d and 5e.

claim: Acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice leads to abnormal serum metabolism.
source: We further found that acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice led to impaired intestinal barrier function, hypoglycemia, and abnormal serum metabolism, which was partly rescued by the Lkb1 loss-induced autophagy upregulation via inhibiting p53 induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by serum metabolomics data shown in Figure 5a-d.

claim: Lkb1 loss-induced autophagy upregulation partly rescues impaired intestinal barrier function, hypoglycemia, and abnormal serum metabolism via inhibiting p53 induction.
source: We further found that acute deletion of Lkb1 in adult mice led to impaired intestinal barrier function, hypoglycemia, and abnormal serum metabolism, which was partly rescued by the Lkb1 loss-induced autophagy upregulation via inhibiting p53 induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice, and by p53 deletion experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Autophagy and Lkb1 work synergistically to maintain adult mouse homeostasis and survival.
source: Taken together, we demonstrated that autophagy and Lkb1 work synergistically to maintain adult mouse homeostasis and survival.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: LKB1 is a tumor suppressor, metabolic sensor, and master modulator of AMPK and mTORC1 activity.
source: Liver kinase B1 (LKB1) is a tumor suppressor, metabolic sensor, and master modulator of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and mammalian target of rapamycin complex1 (mTORC1) activity, leading to the control of energy metabolism, cell polarity, cell survival, and proliferation (Corradetti et al., 2004; Alessi et al., 2006; Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LKB1 controls energy metabolism, cell polarity, cell survival, and proliferation.
source: Liver kinase B1 (LKB1) is a tumor suppressor, metabolic sensor, and master modulator of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and mammalian target of rapamycin complex1 (mTORC1) activity, leading to the control of energy metabolism, cell polarity, cell survival, and proliferation (Corradetti et al., 2004; Alessi et al., 2006; Nakada et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Heterozygous germline mutations in Stk11 lead to the development of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS).
source: Heterozygous germline mutations in Stk11 lead to the development of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), an autosomal dominant disease with hamartomatous polyp formation in the gastrointestinal tract (Giardiello et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal dominant disease with hamartomatous polyp formation in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: Heterozygous germline mutations in Stk11 lead to the development of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS), an autosomal dominant disease with hamartomatous polyp formation in the gastrointestinal tract (Giardiello et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Constitutive deficiency of Lkb1 leads to embryonic lethality due to impaired neural tube closure and somitogenesis, mesenchymal tissue cell death, and defective vasculature.
source: Constitutive deficiency of Lkb1 leads to embryonic lethality due to impaired neural tube closure and somitogenesis, mesenchymal tissue cell death, and defective vasculature (Hardie, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Specific deletion of Lkb1 in vascular endothelial cells results in dilated embryonic vessels and death at E12.5.
source: Specific deletion of Lkb1 in vascular endothelial cells results in dilated embryonic vessels and death at E12.5, which is attributed to the reduced Tgfβ signaling in yolk sac (Corradetti et al., 2004; Londesborough et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Death at E12.5 in vascular endothelial cell-specific Lkb1 deletion is attributed to reduced Tgfβ signaling in yolk sac.
source: Specific deletion of Lkb1 in vascular endothelial cells results in dilated embryonic vessels and death at E12.5, which is attributed to the reduced Tgfβ signaling in yolk sac (Corradetti et al., 2004; Londesborough et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Liver-specific deficiency of Lkb1 causes impaired glucose metabolism.
source: Liver-specific deficiency of Lkb1 causes impaired glucose metabolism (Zhou et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Muscle-specific deletion of Lkb1 results in lower fasting blood glucose and insulin levels, along with increased glucose uptake through muscles.
source: Muscle-specific deletion of Lkb1 results in lower fasting blood glucose and insulin levels, along with increased glucose uptake through muscles (Koh et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lkb1 loss in hematopoietic stem cells causes dysfunctional mitochondria, leading to pancytopenia due to reduced levels of ATP, fatty acids, and nucleotides.
source: Lkb1 loss in hematopoietic stem cells causes dysfunctional mitochondria, leading to pancytopenia due to reduced levels of ATP, fatty acids, and nucleotides (Nakada et al., 2010; Gan et al., 2010; Gurumurthy et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Loss of Lkb1 in intestinal epithelial cells alters immune barrier, changes intestinal colitogenic microbiota, and confers susceptibility to inflammation through reduction of IL-18 via an AMPK-independent pathway.
source: Loss of Lkb1 in intestinal epithelial cells alters immune barrier, changes intestinal colitogenic microbiota, and confers susceptibility to inflammation through reduction of IL-18 via an AMPK-independent pathway (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Somatic Stk11 mutations are related with a number of human cancers.
source: Somatic Stk11 mutations are related with a number of human cancers; however, tissue-specific removal of Stk11 in mice does not necessarily lead to tumor formation (Ollila and Mäkelä, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Tissue-specific removal of Stk11 in mice does not necessarily lead to tumor formation.
source: Somatic Stk11 mutations are related with a number of human cancers; however, tissue-specific removal of Stk11 in mice does not necessarily lead to tumor formation (Ollila and Mäkelä, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Autophagy plays an essential role in cellular stress responses and survival.
source: Autophagy, a highly conserved self-degradative process, plays an essential role in cellular stress responses and survival (Guo et al., 2013; Guo et al., 2016; Komatsu et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Yeast cells rely on autophagy to survive nitrogen starvation.
source: Yeast cells rely on autophagy to survive nitrogen starvation Tsukada and Ohsumi, 1993; neonatal mice depend on autophagy to survive neonatal starvation-induced amino acid depletion (Komatsu et al., 2005; Kuma et al., 2004) and adult mice requires autophagy to survive starvation (Komatsu et al., 2005; Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Neonatal mice depend on autophagy to survive neonatal starvation-induced amino acid depletion.
source: Yeast cells rely on autophagy to survive nitrogen starvation Tsukada and Ohsumi, 1993; neonatal mice depend on autophagy to survive neonatal starvation-induced amino acid depletion (Komatsu et al., 2005; Kuma et al., 2004) and adult mice requires autophagy to survive starvation (Komatsu et al., 2005; Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Adult mice require autophagy to survive starvation.
source: Yeast cells rely on autophagy to survive nitrogen starvation Tsukada and Ohsumi, 1993; neonatal mice depend on autophagy to survive neonatal starvation-induced amino acid depletion (Komatsu et al., 2005; Kuma et al., 2004) and adult mice requires autophagy to survive starvation (Komatsu et al., 2005; Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Systemic Atg7 ablation leads to extensive liver and muscle damage, and neurodegeneration starting at 6 weeks post-deletion.
source: Same as previous report (Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014), systemic Atg7 ablation led to extensive liver and muscle damage, and neurodegeneration starting at 6 weeks post-deletion, and limited mouse survival to 2.5 months.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by the current study.

claim: Systemic Atg7 ablation limits mouse survival to 2.5 months.
source: Same as previous report (Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014), systemic Atg7 ablation led to extensive liver and muscle damage, and neurodegeneration starting at 6 weeks post-deletion, and limited mouse survival to 2.5 months.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by survival data in Figure 2a.

claim: Adult mice with acute ablation of Stk11 through whole-body deletion die within 25 days.
source: Surprisingly, we found that adult mice with acute ablation of Stk11 through whole-body (Stk11-/- mice) died within 25 days and showed upregulated autophagy in most tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Adult mice with acute ablation of Stk11 show upregulated autophagy in most tissues.
source: Surprisingly, we found that adult mice with acute ablation of Stk11 through whole-body (Stk11-/- mice) died within 25 days and showed upregulated autophagy in most tissues.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and IHC data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Systemic co-deletion of Stk11 and Atg7 limits mice survival to 15 days.
source: Moreover, systemic co-deletion of Stk11 and Atg7 limited mice survival to 15 days.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Stk11-/- mice display disruption of intestinal structure and impaired intestinal defense barrier.
source: Stk11-/- mice displayed disruption of intestinal structure and impaired intestinal defense barrier, which was deteriorated by co-deletion with Atg7.
evidence: This claim is supported by histology and FITC-dextran permeability data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Disruption of intestinal structure and impaired intestinal defense barrier in Stk11-/- mice is deteriorated by co-deletion with Atg7.
source: Stk11-/- mice displayed disruption of intestinal structure and impaired intestinal defense barrier, which was deteriorated by co-deletion with Atg7.
evidence: This claim is supported by histology and FITC-dextran permeability data comparing Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice shown in Figure 3.

claim: Supplementation of broad-spectrum antibiotics partly rescues the death of mice with concurrent deletions of Stk11 and Atg7.
source: Supplementation of broad-spectrum antibiotics or systemic deletion of Trp53 partly rescued the death of the mice with concurrent deletions of Stk11 and Atg7, but not the mice with Stk11 deletion alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data with antibiotic treatment shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Systemic deletion of Trp53 partly rescues the death of mice with concurrent deletions of Stk11 and Atg7.
source: Supplementation of broad-spectrum antibiotics or systemic deletion of Trp53 partly rescued the death of the mice with concurrent deletions of Stk11 and Atg7, but not the mice with Stk11 deletion alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data with Trp53 deletion shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Supplementation of broad-spectrum antibiotics does not rescue the death of mice with Stk11 deletion alone.
source: Supplementation of broad-spectrum antibiotics or systemic deletion of Trp53 partly rescued the death of the mice with concurrent deletions of Stk11 and Atg7, but not the mice with Stk11 deletion alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data with antibiotic treatment shown in Figure 3i.

claim: Systemic deletion of Trp53 does not rescue the death of mice with Stk11 deletion alone.
source: Supplementation of broad-spectrum antibiotics or systemic deletion of Trp53 partly rescued the death of the mice with concurrent deletions of Stk11 and Atg7, but not the mice with Stk11 deletion alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data with Trp53 deletion shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Acute short-term deletion of Atg7 or Stk11 significantly decreases the levels of most essential and non-essential amino acids in serum.
source: Serum metabolomics profiling analysis showed that acute short-term deletion of Atg7 or Stk11, respectively, significantly decreased the levels of most essential and non-essential amino acids and some metabolites involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, urea cycle, and glycolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by serum metabolomics data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Acute short-term deletion of Atg7 or Stk11 significantly decreases some metabolites involved in the TCA cycle, urea cycle, and glycolysis.
source: Serum metabolomics profiling analysis showed that acute short-term deletion of Atg7 or Stk11, respectively, significantly decreased the levels of most essential and non-essential amino acids and some metabolites involved in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, urea cycle, and glycolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by serum metabolomics data shown in Figure 5b-d.

claim: The decrease in metabolites is further enhanced in mice with concurrent deletions of Atg7 and Stk11.
source: This phenotype was further enhanced in mice with concurrent deletions of Atg7 and Stk11.
evidence: This claim is supported by serum metabolomics data comparing different genotypes shown in Figure 5.

claim: Autophagy upregulation temporarily compensates for the acute loss of Lkb1.
source: Taken together, this study reveals a novel role of Lkb1 in the management of tissue homeostasis in adult mouse and the mechanism by which autophagy upregulation temporarily compensates for the acute loss of Lkb1.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: TAM injections in 8-10 week-old mice lead to near complete and sustained loss of Atg7 protein in all tissues.
source: Following TAM injections in 8–10 week-old mice, Cre is activated, leading to the deletion of Atg7 or Stk11, and producing a near complete and sustained loss of Atg7 protein (Atg7-/- mice), Lkb1 protein (Stk11-/- mice), or dual deletions of Atg7 and Lkb1 proteins (Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice) in all tissues (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: TAM injections in 8-10 week-old mice lead to near complete and sustained loss of Lkb1 protein in all tissues.
source: Following TAM injections in 8–10 week-old mice, Cre is activated, leading to the deletion of Atg7 or Stk11, and producing a near complete and sustained loss of Atg7 protein (Atg7-/- mice), Lkb1 protein (Stk11-/- mice), or dual deletions of Atg7 and Lkb1 proteins (Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice) in all tissues (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Accumulation of autophagy substrate p62 is observed in all tissues of mice with Atg7 ablation.
source: In addition, accumulation of autophagy substrate p62 was observed in all tissues of the mice with Atg7 ablation (Atg7-/- mice and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice) (Figure 1c), indicating autophagy blockade.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Accumulation of p62 in Atg7-ablated mice indicates autophagy blockade.
source: In addition, accumulation of autophagy substrate p62 was observed in all tissues of the mice with Atg7 ablation (Atg7-/- mice and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice) (Figure 1c), indicating autophagy blockade.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge that p62 accumulates when autophagy is blocked.

claim: AMPK can be activated by calmodulin-dependent kinase kinase (CaMKK) and transforming growth factor beta-activated kinase1 (TAK1) instead of Lkb1.
source: Instead of Lkb1, AMPK can be activated by calmodulin-dependent kinase kinase (CaMKK) and transforming growth factor beta-activated kinase1 (TAK1) (Hardie, 2011; Sanders et al., 2007), further leading to autophagy activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of AMPK by CaMKK and TAK1 leads to autophagy activation.
source: Instead of Lkb1, AMPK can be activated by calmodulin-dependent kinase kinase (CaMKK) and transforming growth factor beta-activated kinase1 (TAK1) (Hardie, 2011; Sanders et al., 2007), further leading to autophagy activation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and established knowledge.

claim: pAMPK (T172) is observed in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice.
source: As expected, pAMPK (T172) was observed in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Phosphorylation of ULK1 (S555) and ACC (S79) is detected in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice.
source: Consistent with AMPK activation, phosphorylation of ULK1 (S555) and ACC (S79) was also detected in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and IHC data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: pS6 is significantly reduced in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice compared with WT mice.
source: Most interestingly, although pAMPK was not further increased in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice, pS6 which indicates the activation of mTORC1 signaling was significantly reduced in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice compared with WT mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and IHC data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: The level of pULK1(S757) is reduced in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice compared with WT mice.
source: With the decrease of pS6, the level of pULK1(S757), a phosphorylation site by mTORC1 (Egan et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2011), was reduced in the tissues of Stk11-/- mice compared with WT mice (Figure 1d and e, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot and IHC data shown in Figure 1d and 1e.

claim: Atg5-Atg12 conjugation is observed in most tissues of Stk11-/- mice.
source: Moreover, Atg5-Atg12 conjugation was observed in the most tissues of Stk11-/- mice (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: HCQ treatment leads to accumulation of LC3-II and p62 in most tissues of mice.
source: Accumulation of autophagy substrates including both microtubule-associated protein 1A/1B- light chain3 (LC3) I and II along with p62 was observed in most tissues of mice after 5 hr of HCQ treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: HCQ treatment leads to higher accumulation of LC3-II and p62 in Stk11-deficient mice compared with WT control mice.
source: Moreover, HCQ treatment led to a higher accumulation of LC3-II and p62 in Stk11-deficient mice compared with WT control mice (Figure 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Autophagy is activated and upregulated in mice with acute loss of Lkb1.
source: Taken together, we demonstrated that autophagy is activated and upregulated in the mice with acute loss of Lkb1.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by multiple experimental findings shown in Figure 1.

claim: Mice with systemic autophagy ablation have a life span of 2-3 months.
source: It has previously been shown that mice with systemic autophagy ablation have a life span of 2–3 months and the mortality is due to initial Streptococcus infection and eventual neurodegeneration (Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014), whereas, adult mice with whole-body Stk11 deletion survive for up to 6 weeks (Shan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The mortality of mice with systemic autophagy ablation is due to initial Streptococcus infection and eventual neurodegeneration.
source: It has previously been shown that mice with systemic autophagy ablation have a life span of 2–3 months and the mortality is due to initial Streptococcus infection and eventual neurodegeneration (Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014), whereas, adult mice with whole-body Stk11 deletion survive for up to 6 weeks (Shan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult mice with whole-body Stk11 deletion survive for up to 6 weeks.
source: It has previously been shown that mice with systemic autophagy ablation have a life span of 2–3 months and the mortality is due to initial Streptococcus infection and eventual neurodegeneration (Karsli-Uzunbas et al., 2014), whereas, adult mice with whole-body Stk11 deletion survive for up to 6 weeks (Shan et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The life span of Stk11-deficient mice is limited to 3.5 weeks post-TAM administration.
source: The life span of Stk11-deficient mice was limited to 3.5 weeks post-TAM administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Co-deletion of Atg7 and Stk11 results in 2 weeks of survival.
source: Co-deletion of Atg7 and Stk11 led to a significant decrease in the survival of Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with Stk11-/- or Atg7-/- mice, resulting 2 weeks of survival (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: There is a loss of body weight in Stk11-/- mice at 10 days post-TAM injection compared with WT control mice.
source: At 10 days post-TAM injection, compared with WT control mice, there was a loss of body weight in Stk11-/- mice, which was significantly deteriorated by the loss of Atg7 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Body weight loss in Stk11-/- mice is significantly deteriorated by the loss of Atg7.
source: At 10 days post-TAM injection, compared with WT control mice, there was a loss of body weight in Stk11-/- mice, which was significantly deteriorated by the loss of Atg7 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Hematopoietic-specific Stk11-deficient mice die from pancytopenia.
source: Hematopoietic-specific Stk11-deficient mice died from pancytopenia (Gan et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: No differences in red and white blood cell and platelet count are observed among WT control, Atg7-/-, and Stk11-/- mice.
source: We did not observe any differences of red and white blood cell and platelet count among WT control, Atg7-/-, and Stk11-/- mice; however, the platelet count in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice was significantly higher than that in WT control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by blood count data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The platelet count in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice is significantly higher than that in WT control mice.
source: We did not observe any differences of red and white blood cell and platelet count among WT control, Atg7-/-, and Stk11-/- mice; however, the platelet count in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice was significantly higher than that in WT control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by blood count data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: After short-period (10 days) of protein deletion, tissue damage is not observed in Atg7-deficient mice.
source: After short-period (10 days) of protein deletion, which is before the death of Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice, the damage of tissues was not observed in Atg7-deficient mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Most tissues in both Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice are not visibly affected except for the intestine.
source: Moreover, except for the intestine (Figure 3a), most of the tissues in both Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice were not visibly affected as examined by hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Tissue-specific Stk11 deletion in intestinal-epithelium cells results in enlarged undifferentiated goblet-Paneth cells in the crypt of intestine.
source: Same as tissue-specific Stk11 deletion in intestinal-epithelium cells (Shorning et al., 2009), enlarged undifferentiated goblet-Paneth cells in the crypt of intestine, including duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, were observed in Stk11-/- mice, which was further exacerbated by the concurrent ablation of Atg7 in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and confirmed by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Enlarged undifferentiated goblet-Paneth cells in the crypt of intestine are observed in Stk11-/- mice.
source: Same as tissue-specific Stk11 deletion in intestinal-epithelium cells (Shorning et al., 2009), enlarged undifferentiated goblet-Paneth cells in the crypt of intestine, including duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, were observed in Stk11-/- mice, which was further exacerbated by the concurrent ablation of Atg7 in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Enlarged undifferentiated goblet-Paneth cells in Stk11-/- mice are further exacerbated by concurrent ablation of Atg7.
source: Same as tissue-specific Stk11 deletion in intestinal-epithelium cells (Shorning et al., 2009), enlarged undifferentiated goblet-Paneth cells in the crypt of intestine, including duodenum, jejunum, and ileum, were observed in Stk11-/- mice, which was further exacerbated by the concurrent ablation of Atg7 in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by H&E staining data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The decreased intensity of lysozyme staining indicates less frequent and undifferentiated Paneth cells in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice.
source: The decreased intensity of lysozyme staining indicates less frequent and undifferentiated Paneth cells in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: LC3-II puncta are observed in the intestine of Stk11-/- mice.
source: In consistent with the induction of autophagy in Stk11-deficient mice, LC3-II puncta were observed in the intestine of Stk11-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Lkb1 is involved in the development and maintenance of goblet and Paneth cells.
source: Lkb1 is involved in the development and maintenance of the goblet and Paneth cells (Shorning et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Specific deletion of Stk11 in intestinal stem cells leads to increased expression of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase4 and reduced oxygen consumption.
source: Specific deletion of Stk11 in intestinal stem cells leads to increased expression of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase4 and reduced oxygen consumption, which reduces the population of stem cells and increase the levels of secretory cell number (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Specific deletion of Stk11 in intestinal stem cells reduces the population of stem cells and increases the levels of secretory cell number.
source: Specific deletion of Stk11 in intestinal stem cells leads to increased expression of pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase4 and reduced oxygen consumption, which reduces the population of stem cells and increase the levels of secretory cell number (Gao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The impaired goblet and Paneth cells are characteristics of PJS in humans.
source: The impaired goblet and Paneth cells are also characteristics of PJS in humans (Udd et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The impaired intestinal structure is further exaggerated when Atg7 is concurrently deleted with Stk11.
source: Additionally, we found that the impaired intestinal structure was further exaggerated when Atg7 is concurrently deleted with Stk11.
evidence: This claim is supported by histology data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The major function of Goblet cells is attributed to the secretion of mucus to provide the epithelium immune barrier against bacterial invasion from the intestinal lumen.
source: The major function of Goblet cells is attributed to the secretion of mucus to provide the epithelium immune barrier against bacterial invasion from the intestinal lumen (Birchenough et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Lkb1 loss leads to the deficiency of immune barrier through an AMPK-independent pathway which is required for the production of antimicrobial IL-18.
source: Moreover, Lkb1 loss leads to the deficiency of immune barrier through an AMPK-independent pathway which is required for the production of antimicrobial IL-18 (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The integrity of intestinal-epithelium barrier and function are damaged with a greater extent in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with Stk11-/- mice.
source: Here we demonstrated that the integrity of intestinal-epithelium barrier and function are damaged with a greater extent in Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with Stk11-/- mice, leaving the mice vulnerable to infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by FITC-dextran permeability data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The role of autophagy in microbial defense is well established.
source: The role of autophagy in microbial defense is well established (Gutierrez et al., 2007; Tan et al., 2009; Terebiznik et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: One of the main roles of intestinal epithelium autophagy is to engulf invaded bacteria from extra intestinal sites, which is implied by innate immune adaptor protein MyD88.
source: One of the main roles of intestinal epithelium autophagy is to engulf invaded bacteria from extra intestinal sites, which is implied by innate immune adaptor protein MyD88 (Benjamin et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Autophagy is crucial for the function of Paneth cells.

claim: The lower intensity and frequency of cells expressing OLFM4 are observed in Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with WT control or Atg7-/- mice.
source: IHC for olfactomedin4 (OLFM4) (an intestine stem cell marker) shows the lower intensity and frequency of the cells expressing OLFM4 in Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with WT control or Atg7-/- mice (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Intestinal stem cells reside at the bottom of the crypt for regenerating almost all the epithelium cells, including Paneth and goblet cells, enterocytes and tuft cells.
source: To evaluate the role of Lkb1 and autophagy in other components of the small intestinal crypt, we examined the status of stem cells that reside at the bottom of the crypt for regenerating almost all the epithelium cells, including Paneth and goblet cells, enterocytes and tuft cells (Birchenough et al., 2015; Clevers, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cell death in small intestine occurs through apoptosis mostly at the tip of the villi which eventually leads to shedding of dead cells into the lumen.
source: Cell death in small intestine occurs through apoptosis mostly at the tip of the villi which eventually leads to shedding of dead cells into the lumen (Blander, 2016; Günther et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Intestinal crypt is the region for cell division and migration to upper sites of the villi.
source: Intestinal crypt is the region for cell division and migration to upper sites of the villi (Parker et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The reduced levels of TCA cycle intermediates are only observed in the absence of Atg7 (Atg7-/- mice and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice), but not in Stk11-deficient mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that the reduced levels of TCA cycle intermediates were only observed in the absence of Atg7 (Atg7-/- mice and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice), but not in Stk11-deficient mice (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by serum metabolomics data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Blood glucose level is significantly lower in Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with WT control mice in both fasted and fed states.
source: We further found that in both fasted state (Figure 5d) and fed state (Figure 5e), blood glucose level was significantly lower in Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice compared with WT control mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 5d and 5e.

claim: The insulin levels in Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice are decreased with the same trend as glucose compared with WT control mice.
source: The insulin levels in Stk11-/- and Atg7-/-;Stk11-/- mice were decreased with the same trend as glucose compared with WT control mice (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by serum insulin measurements shown in Figure 5f.
